title: Home, things, and whose is whose
title_target: ເຮືອນ ແລະ ຂອງໃຜ — Hʉan lae khǎwng phǎi
goal: Describe where you live, say what there is and isn't, say who owns what, and find lost things — while setting up Lao's three distance demonstratives.

positions: ເທິງ ລຸ່ມ ໃນ ນອກ ຂ້າງ

dialogs.title: ບົດສົນທະນາ — The lost key in the office
dialogs.intro: Budi has lost his room key. Notice how the demonstratives change according to who is closer to the object — not just how far it is from the speaker.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ບຸນມີ|Bun-míi] [ເຫັນ|hěn][ກະແຈ|ka-jèe][ຂ້ອຍ|khàwy][ບໍ່|bàw] [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ເສຍ|sǐa][ແລ້ວ|lèeo]
lines.id: Bounmy, have you seen my key? I've lost it.
lines.literal: Bounmy — see — key — I — (question)? I — lose — already.

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ກະແຈ|Ka-jèe][ໃດ|dai] [ອັນ|An][ນີ້|nîi][ບໍ່|bàw]
lines.id: Which key? Is it this one?

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ບໍ່ແມ່ນ|Bàw mèen] [ອັນ|An][ນັ້ນ|nân][ຂອງ|khǎwng][ເຈົ້າ|jâo] [ຂອງ|Khǎwng][ຂ້ອຍ|khàwy][ສີ|sǐi][ດຳ|dam]
lines.id: No. That one's yours. Mine is black.
lines.literal: not. piece — that — of — you. of — I — color — black.

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ຢູ່|Yùu][ເທິງ|thóeng][ໂຕະ|tó][ບໍ່|bàw] [ຫຼື|Lʉ̌ʉ][ຢູ່|yùu][ໃນ|nai][ຖົງ|thǒng]
lines.id: Is it on the desk? Or in your bag?
lines.literal: be-at — on — table — (question)? or — be-at — in — bag?

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ບໍ່ມີ|Bàw míi] [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ຫາ|hǎa][ແລ້ວ|lèeo] [ຢູ່|Yùu][ລຸ່ມ|lùm][ຕັ່ງ|tàng][ກໍ|kaw][ບໍ່ມີ|bàw míi]
lines.id: It's not there. I've looked. It's not under the chair either.
lines.literal: not — have. I — look-for — already. be-at — under — chair — also — not — have.

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ເບິ່ງ|Bòeng][ພຸ້ນ|phûn][ແດ່|dèe] [ຢູ່|Yùu][ຂ້າງ|khàang][ຄອມ|khawm][ພຸ້ນ|phûn] [ແມ່ນ|Mèen][ບໍ່|bàw]
lines.id: Try looking over there. Next to that computer. Isn't that it?
lines.literal: look — over-there — a-bit. be-at — beside — compu — over-there. right — (question)?

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ແມ່ນ|Mèen][ແລ້ວ|lèeo] [ຂອບໃຈ|Khàwp-jai][ຫຼາຍໆ|lǎai-lǎai] [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ຂີ້ລືມ|khîi-lʉʉm][ຫຼາຍ|lǎai]
lines.id: That's it! Thanks so much. I'm so forgetful.
lines.literal: right — already. thank-you — much-much. I — forgetful — much.

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ບໍ່ເປັນຫຍັງ|Bàw pen nyǎng] [ເຮືອນ|Hʉan][ເຈົ້າ|jâo][ເປັນ|pen][ແນວ|neeo][ໃດ|dai] [ໃຫຍ່|Nyài][ບໍ່|bàw]
lines.id: No problem. What's your place like? Is it big?
lines.literal: not — be — what. house — you — be — way — which? big — (question)?

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ບໍ່|Bàw][ໃຫຍ່|nyài] [ມີ|Míi][ສອງ|sǎwng][ຫ້ອງ|hàwng] [ຫ້ອງ|Hàwng][ນອນ|náwn][ກັບ|kap][ຫ້ອງ|hàwng][ຄົວ|khúa] [ແຕ່|Tèe][ບໍ່ມີ|bàw míi][ເຄື່ອງ|khʉ̂ang][ແອ|ee]
lines.id: Not big. There are two rooms: a bedroom and a kitchen. But there's no AC.
lines.literal: not — big. have — two — room. room — sleep — with — room — cook. but — not — have — machine — cool.

lines.speaker: ບຸນມີ:
lines.text: [ບໍ່ມີ|Bàw míi][ເຄື່ອງແອ|khʉ̂ang-ee][ຮ້ອນ|hâwn][ບໍ່|bàw]

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ຮ້ອນ|Hâwn][ຢູ່|yùu] [ແຕ່|Tèe][ມີ|míi][ພັດລົມ|phat-lóm][ສອງ|sǎwng][ໜ່ວຍ|nùay] [ພໍ|Phaw][ໄດ້|dâi]
lines.id: It is hot. But I have two fans. It'll do.
lines.literal: hot — (ongoing). but — have — fan — two — piece. enough — can.

notes: **ມີ míi means both "there is" AND "to have" — one word for both.** English splits these, Lao doesn't. *ຂ້ອຍມີລົດ* (I have a car), *ຢູ່ນີ້ມີຮ້ານກາເຟ* (there's a coffee shop here). The negative is *ບໍ່ມີ bàw míi*, one of the sentences you'll hear and say most.
**ຂອງໃຜ khǎwng phǎi = "whose."** The answer: *ຂອງຂ້ອຍ* (mine), *ຂອງລາວ* (his/hers). In fast speech *ຂອງ* is often dropped before the person: *ກະແຈຂ້ອຍ* is enough for "my key."

**Three distances, not two.** *ນີ້ nîi* = near the speaker (this). *ນັ້ນ nân* = near the listener (that). *ພຸ້ນ phûn* = far from both (that over there). Modern English uses "that" for the last two; Lao keeps them apart, like the old English "yonder."
**Demonstratives come AFTER the noun.** *ກະແຈອັນນີ້* (this key), *ຄົນນັ້ນ* (that person), *ເຮືອນພຸ້ນ* (that house over there). For objects, a classifier slips in between: *ອັນນີ້*, *ໂຕນັ້ນ*.
**ເສຍ sǐa = "lost, broken, wasted."** *ກະແຈເສຍ* (the key is lost), *ລົດເສຍ* (the car broke down), *ເສຍເງິນ* (lose money), *ເສຍໃຈ sǐa-jai* (sad, literally "lose heart"). One word, many losses.
**ຫາ hǎa = "to look for."** *ຫາກະແຈ* (look for the key). The same word means "to" in *ໂທຫາ thóo hǎa* (to call someone). And *ພົບ phop* or *ເຫັນ hěn* for "find, see": *ພົບແລ້ວ* (found it).
**ພໍໄດ້ phaw dâi = "it'll do, not bad."** A very Lao way to accept things as they are, without complaining or praising. Its twin: *ພໍໃຊ້ໄດ້ phaw sâi dâi* (good enough to use).
**ຂີ້ລືມ khîi-lʉʉm = "forgetful."** Remember the prefix *ຂີ້-* from Unit 9, which marks habits. *ຂ້ອຍຂີ້ລືມ* is a light apology that's almost always answered with a laugh.
**ຢູ່ yùu at the end of a sentence means "it is (right now)."** *ຮ້ອນຢູ່* = "it is hot" — acknowledging an ongoing state. This is the third use of *ຢູ່*, after "to be at" and "at/in."

grammars.title: Positions: eight words that cover everything

head: Lao
Say it
English
Example
rows: *ຢູ່ເທິງໂຕະ* — on the table
*ຢູ່ລຸ່ມຕັ່ງ* — under the chair
*ຢູ່ໃນຖົງ* — in the bag
*ຢູ່ນອກເຮືອນ* — outside the house
*ຢູ່ຂ້າງປະຕູ* — next to the door
*ຢູ່ໜ້າຮ້ານ* — in front of the shop
*ຢູ່ຫຼັງເຮືອນ* — behind the house
*ຢູ່ລະຫວ່າງສອງເຮືອນ*

after: All of them are used with *ຢູ່ yùu* in front. Without *ຢູ່*, these words become nouns: *ເທິງ* (the top), *ໃນ* (the inside).

grammars.title: Saying who owns what

head: Lao
Say it
Meaning
rows: ອັນນີ້ຂອງໃຜ
ຂອງຂ້ອຍເອງ
ບໍ່ແມ່ນຂອງຂ້ອຍ
ກະແຈຂອງບຸນມີ
ໜ້າຈະແມ່ນຂອງລາວ
can I borrow it for a moment?

after: **ເອງ *éeng*** means "self" and adds emphasis: *ຂອງຂ້ອຍເອງ* (my very own), *ເຮັດເອງ* (made it myself), *ໄປເອງ* (go by myself).
**ໜ້າຈະ *nâa-ja*** = "probably, most likely." It softens a guess so you don't sound accusing — very handy when people's things get mixed up.

sections.title: The house and what's in it

head: Lao
Say it
English
Lao
Say it
English
rows: ຫ້ອງຮັບແຂກ

blocks.text: Notice **ຫ້ອງ *hàwng***, meaning "room," which goes in front of its function: *ຫ້ອງນອນ* (sleep room), *ຫ້ອງຄົວ* (cooking room), *ຫ້ອງນ້ຳ* (water room = bathroom/restroom), *ຫ້ອງການ hàwng-kaan* (work room = office). Much like English *bedroom* and *bathroom*, just with the parts the other way around.

A traditional Lao house — *ເຮືອນລາວ* — stands on stilts, with open space underneath for working and escaping the heat. If you're invited in, **take off your shoes at the stairs** and don't step on the threshold; in local belief it's where the house's guardian spirit lives.
